answer.exemplar: A reference angle is the acute angle between the terminal side of the given angle and the nearest horizontal axis, and it is always positive and never larger than pi/2. To find one, first decide which quadrant the angle lies in. An angle already between 0 and pi/2, or between 3pi/2 and 2pi, is itself its own reference angle. In the second quadrant subtract the angle from pi, in the third quadrant subtract it from pi as well, and in the fourth quadrant subtract it from 2pi, always keeping the positive remainder. The reference angle on its own does not give the value of sine or cosine, because the coordinate being read off the unit circle changes sign from one quadrant to the next. Sine reads the y-coordinate, which is positive above the x-axis and negative below it, so sine is positive in the first and second quadrants and negative in the third and fourth. Cosine reads the x-coordinate, which is positive to the right of the y-axis and negative to the left of it, so cosine is positive in the first and fourth quadrants and negative in the second and third. The working rule is therefore to take the exact trigonometric value at the reference angle and then apply the sign that the quadrant demands, and the sign of the tangent is decided by dividing the two signs rather than by a rule of its own.

answer.exemplar: In the form y = A sin(Bx + C) + D each symbol controls one visible property of the graph and nothing else, so the description can be read straight off. The coefficient A standing outside the brackets is the amplitude, and its magnitude is what counts, because a negative A flips the wave upside down as well as setting its height. The factor B inside the brackets stretches or compresses the wave horizontally, and the period is 2 pi divided by the magnitude of B, since the argument has to advance through a full 2 pi before the wave repeats itself. The constant C inside the brackets gives the phase shift once the bracket is written as Bx minus h, in which case the graph slides h radians to the right, and a plus sign inside the bracket slides it left by the same amount. The constant D on the end is the vertical shift, and it sets the midline, so the graph runs from D minus the amplitude to D plus the amplitude. Reading those four values in that order, and keeping track of the fact that a sign change is attached to the amplitude, gives a complete description of the transformed wave without drawing it.

answer.exemplar: The addition formula reads cos(A + B) = cos A cos B - sin A sin B. To turn it into the difference formula, replace B with -B, which leaves cos(A - B) = cos A cos(-B) - sin A sin(-B) on the page. Cosine is an even function, so cos(-B) equals cos B and the first product is untouched, while sine is an odd function, so sin(-B) equals -sin B. That negative then combines with the minus sign already in front of the second product and the two become a plus, which gives cos(A - B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B, with the two sine terms now joined by addition. The same substitution applied to sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B produces sin(A - B) = sin A cos B - cos A sin B, so in each formula the term that changes sign is the one built from the odd function. Setting A equal to B is the check that both formulas are right, since the difference formula should then return cos 0 equal to 1 and sin 0 equal to 0, which it does for either sign arrangement of the wrong version.

answer.exemplar: Sine is periodic with period 2 pi, so once any one solution is found, adding a whole multiple of 2 pi to it produces another, and there is no largest such multiple to add. The principal value is t = arcsin(0.7), which is about 0.7754 radians, and because sine takes the value 0.7 twice in every period the general solution has two families, t = 0.7754 + 2n pi and t = 2.3662 + 2n pi, for any integer n. Each family is infinite in both directions because n ranges over all whole numbers, so the equation has infinitely many solutions rather than two. The claim of two comes from counting the solutions inside a single period, from 0 to 2 pi, and then stopping. That count would be correct for a question that restricted t to one period and wrong for any question about all real values of t, which is what the report was about. The contradiction can also be seen directly, since sine of t plus 2 pi equals sine of t for every t, so 0.7754, 0.7754 + 2 pi and 0.7754 + 4 pi are all distinct numbers with the same sine, and repeating the argument never exhausts them.
